utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber understood that you would like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would, yes. I've got two or three points, Your Honour. The first one --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I've got two or three points, Your Honour. The first one, and I should say straight away that unusually it's a matter on which I've not consulted anyone on my team. It's this, Your Honour, over the long weekend that we have had, I thought about Friday, the content of Friday's court hearing and I thought about a number of aspects of Friday's court hearing. Your Honour, the sometimes the temperature between you with respect, Judge Orie, and me, is not a happy one and, Your Honour, I apologise for my contribution to that, whether my contribution has been the magic 60 per cent, 70 per cent, 100 per cent or 105 per cent, Your Honour has two things, my apology for my contribution to that in the past, because it's an undoubted fact, Your Honour, I acknowledge that, and secondly my assurance and my resolve to try to stop it immediately as far as I possibly can. And that's all I have to say on that, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. The second point is this, Your Honour, that we have an application for leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just to make sure that the record is complete, I had my microphone not switched on and when I said it's accepted, therefore, it did not appear and I find it important that it appears that I have accepted what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Your Honour. I heard it and registered it, Your Honour. I'm glad for it to be seen more widely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have an application or we have an application, the Defence, Your Honour, for leave to reply to the response filed yesterday by the Prosecution to the Defence motion for time to call further witnesses and, Your Honour, because we appreciate that this is a matter which clearly needs to be dealt with, with dispatch, and I'm sure Your Honours will want to do that, Your Honour, we are asking for leave in circumstances where we are ready immediately to file that. It is prepared, it is signed, it is done and dusted, and so we don't hold Your Honours up it will be filed straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Your Honour. Much obliged for that. Your Honour, the third matter is this, and it does as it happens arise from Friday. Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik, we saw him at the UNDU yesterday, Mr. Krajisnik has asked me, Your Honour, and we regard that as constructive, that he's asked me to do it, he's asked me to express his extreme concern and unhappiness about the reaction and about the way that his proposed questioning of Mrs. Plavsic was dealt with on Friday. Mr. Krajisnik does feel, and Your Honour, without wishing to stir up the temperature, Your Honour, I will say that the Defence counsel do endorse this with our submission, Your Honour, do feel that Mr. Krajisnik was rather peremptorily cut off, that the initial introductory remark that he made to his questioning was really no different from remarks which are very commonly made by counsel or even, dare I say, by judges as a brief introduction to questions, and Your Honour we simply invite Your Honour -- it's all a bit done and dusted again so far as that aspect of the matter is concerned, Mrs. Plavsic has gone back, but we would wish Your Honour to understand at the very beginning of that exchange does appear to have involved a rather sharp cutting off of Mr. Krajisnik in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without giving a full response to that matter at this moment, Mr. Stewart, I just at least draw your attention to two facts. First of all, that because of the personal relationship between -- in the past between Mr. Krajisnik and Mrs. Plavsic, that the Chamber indicated that it would be very strict on the matter. And just to point at another example is that I've never heard a witness being addressed by his or her first name rather than by witness so and so or by their family name which is one of the things that was right at the beginning of the introduction of the first questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hear that and Mr. Krajisnik hears that, Your Honour. I'm going to say nothing whatever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then having dealt with that, I'd like to turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Puric, now I'd like to ask you to stand up for a second. Before you give evidence before this Tribunal, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puric. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, would you be -- please be so kind to give us your -- to state your full name?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: My name is Emin Puric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric your date of birth is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: The 8th of June 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the place where you reside at present is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puric. I would like to show you a photograph. Could D116A be put on the ELMO? Mr. Puric, do you recognise the situation we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise some people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us perhaps starting at the left, the first person with a -- with glasses, that is --

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I think that is Amir Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the person standing next to him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Next to him, I cannot tell because it's so dark. I simply cannot. I cannot see the face clearly. I cannot say who it is. The next person is Radomir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and when you say the next person you mean the next person in that same row and not the persons behind, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No, not behind that person, but in the same line, the third person on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These understood. And then next to him also a person wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think the name was Mr. Jens. He was a representative of the international community. He talked to us about the problem of staying in or leaving Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the person next to him with his hand near to his face?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Hand on his face, the commander of the police in Dvor. Right now, I cannot recall the name. I knew him -- I knew the name before I walked into this courtroom and now I cannot remember for the life of me. But I know that he was the chief of police in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Usher, could you please have the full photograph visible on the screen by zooming out a bit? And the last person in that same line, with a clearly visible watch on his left wrist, Mr. Puric, could you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: It's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you perhaps briefly describe the situation, what happened when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: When this photograph was taken, we were on a bridge, the bridge on the Una River, that separates Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croatia. We were talking about the possibility of a convoy leaving Bosanski Novi and going to Croatia. Before that, we had a discussion at my home, a few days before this. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you there. When you say "we had a discussion at my home," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, I've given you the names and surnames, but together with some other people, I tried to establish contact with the international force of the UN that was in Dvor so that they would help us leave this hell in Bosanski Novi where we were under siege. In actual fact, a few people met up who lived in houses close to my own. It's not that we could have had a bigger gathering because there was a general blockade. Amir Delic, Ceric Azemir and I raised the issue of the entire population leaving Bosanski Novi. In a way, I was the person who coordinated that team and who established contact with the authorities in Bosanski Novi regarding that particular idea. May I proceed along these lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. We might have a few additional questions at a later stage but please continue to briefly explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: In order to make it clear as to how necessary it was to leave or, rather, how necessary it was for the entire Bosnian population to leave, I would have to tell the Honourable Trial Chamber what was going on at the time with the Bosniak population in Bosanski Novi and in the surrounding area. With your permission, I would like to start with the month of April roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first would like to put some additional questions to you in relation to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were meeting on that bridge. Was that the only meeting on the bridge or have there been more meetings on that bridge?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: There was another meeting at the bridge too. There were certainly more meetings. And there was this meeting in my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the meeting in your house --

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there one meeting or have there been more meetings in your house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: There were two meetings in my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you just --

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I have not said anything yet. You said you tried to establish contact with the international force of the UN that was in Dvor so that they would help to you leave Bosanski Novi. Did the -- did any representative of the international force or the international community ever come to your house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I think Mr. Jens, who is in the photograph, was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also told us that you were coordinating the team and that you established contact with the authorities in Bosanski Novi about the Bosniak population to leave Bosanski Novi. Were you in any way formally representing the -- representing the -- who gave you the authority to act on behalf of the Bosniak population?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No. There was no formal representation. This was simply because I knew the people from the municipality better, and I called a former colleague of mine from work. He worked together with me for a long time in the same company where I worked. At that time he was president of the Executive Board. I asked him to receive us. I phoned him at his home. I had his home telephone number because we had been in touch before that too, as we knew each other personally and we were great friends, as a matter of fact. I asked him to receive us, I said that we wanted to talk about something that was very important for us. He said that there was no problem and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who that person was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: That person is Dragomir Drazic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember when exactly you got the idea to approach him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: It is very hard to say when I got that idea to approach him. For a long time we were in isolation in our yards, in our homes. When we looked at the possibility of leaving, the three people I mentioned talked about this, Delic, Amir, I, and another man called Ceric Asmir. We are next-door neighbours. We wanted to leave, but we wanted to help other people too, those people who wanted to save their lives. It wasn't that we made any announcements to that effect that we were calling upon people to leave. We kept this secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember when you got in touch with Mr. Drazic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date exactly but it was the beginning of June, around that time. That's when it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until that moment, would people be allowed to leave Bosanski Novi if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: You know, some people were leaving, but they left by paying a Serb who was in uniform for that, more or less everybody had uniforms. They paid in order to be allowed to leave. At first it was 1.000 Deutschmarks per person and then they would take either that person's vehicle or their own vehicle and they would be taken out together with their entire families from Bosanski Novi via Dvor, Glina, Vojnic, towards Karlovac. People were leaving that way. There were several such cases. We heard about these departures. However, most people could not pay that kind of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how did Mr. Drazic respond to your -- to you approaching him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all he received us very nicely. He said that quite simply he did not want to take part in any such thing but that he was not opposed at all to us leaving if we wanted to leave. I asked that no problems be made for us if we wanted to leave town and to go to Dvor. He said that he cannot do much about that but that he cannot help us go to Dvor either, that we should resort to our own ways and means, and indeed we did. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us with whom you further had any contact in this matter. Yes, and perhaps Judge Hanoteau has one question in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to know what was Mr. Drazic exactly? Who was he? What was his profession? Did he play a political role in some way?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drazic had a degree in law. At the time when I worked at the knitwear factory, he also had a responsible job and that's when we got to know each other and we were on such good terms. At that time, he was president of the executive board of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, I think he was president of the executive board, because for a while when this war started, we were not exactly in touch, and I don't know about this month or two when we re-established contact, I don't think there were any changes in the meantime. I think he was still president of the executive board. His political role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please continue and answer the question I did put to you that, apart from Mr. Drazic, who you addressed in this matter?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: As for this particular question, we did not discuss it with anyone else in the municipality. Our only contacts with other people were on the bridge. That was the president of the municipality, Predrag Pasic or, rather, Radomir Pasic, this gentleman who is in the photograph. We had a contact with him only during these negotiations at the bridge. That was the only case. Also we did not communicate with Drazic any more. As a matter of fact, we did not talk to Drazic at all at the bridge. He was quite reticent. He did not really take part in the negotiations at the bridge. Only when they came to my home before that, Mr. Drazic brought them, brought Mr. Jens and the journalists who were accompanying Mr. Jens, together with an interpreter. Actually that was the first time they came to my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When Mr. Drazic said that he did not oppose your suggestion, did he do so spontaneously, immediately? Did he get in touch with anyone before doing so? Could you tell us whether you got his response right away?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked for about an hour, perhaps a bit more, about these problems and so on and so forth. He said, as far as I'm concerned I don't mind at all. But we insisted that he confirm that with his people at the municipality, that they give their approval. I knew that he was not the one who could approve that for us only on his own. That is why I asked him to establish contact with other people too and to familiarise the then Crisis Staff with that. There was a Crisis Staff at the time, and the Crisis Staff was the body that knew of all these moves and that made all the decisions at the time. That is why I asked him to confirm this for us later and indeed he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us that -- let me just find it -- that Mr. Jens was involved and that he visited you at your place.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the first time you met him or was the first time that you had contact with a representative of the international community?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Jens first came to my house that time, but my first contact with the representatives of the international community took place in Dvor. I cannot recall the face of that man. I don't think it was Jens. I think it was a younger gentleman. You know, those were very stressful times. We were afraid at the time. We were afraid when we were there, when we passed by those guards and we had to, near Bosanski Novi, so if I were to be shown a photograph of the representative of the international community in Dvor, I could not recognise him but I know full well that Mr. Jens came to my house and that he was present during the talks at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you go to Dvor once? Did you go there more than once?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I went there twice. We went there twice. As a matter of fact, after we went there for the first time -- perhaps I could say a few words about what we discussed there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, I said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: In order to get to Dvor, we had to do it illegally because we could not get any kind of pass. So we asked a man, a friend of ours, a Serb, and he took a little car and drove us there. That is the smallest possible car. And Amir Delic and I sat there so he sat in this car called Peglica and at the bridge we were stopped by the guards of the Republic of the Srpska Krajina. He spoke a few words to them and he sort of made a joke and they didn't ask any further questions as to who it was that was travelling with him and they let us go. Knowing where the UNPROFOR was at the time, we went to the hotel. When we came to the hotel, we asked for the people who were in charge so that we could talk to them. The interpreter said that they were not there at the moment and that we could come the following day. I said that on the following day we probably would not be able to come so could we please just stay there and wait. And they said, fine, if you want to wait here. We waited for a few hours. I don't know exactly how long it was. When they got back, then we started talking to them. They asked why -- I mean they asked what we wanted and then I first described the situation in Bosanski Novi that every day or every other day people were being taken away for some kind of interviews at the hotel or the fire brigade building or the police, that many people never came back, that we hear that they were beaten, beaten very badly, and so on and so forth, that there were murders in town and in the surrounding area. Also that there is a camp at the sports stadium of the Sloboda football club and so on and so forth. We described the entire situation as it was. And we said that we wanted to leave in a collective way. That is to say that all citizens who wished to leave would leave and we wanted them to help us leave Bosanski Novi. That would be the first discussion we had briefly. They took some kind of notes. I think that even a record was compiled. They asked us whether we were willing to sign that and I said, why not? Everything I said is true. We signed it, Amir Delic and I signed it. They took pictures of us, I don't know why, and they said,"You can go home and we'll come. We'll come and we'll see what can be done. We'll talk to the authorities." However, a week went by, for sure, perhaps even eight days or 10 days, I can't say exactly and they never came. Again, the same people, Amir Delic, Azemir Ceric, and my other next door neighbours, we were wondering what to do then. No one was coming. We felt lost. People were coming and asking questions already because people found out that it was possible to leave collectively and then they were phoning and asking. Every day, it became more and more difficult to leave. That is to say, people who took others out raised their prices from 1.000 Deutschmark, the price went up to 2, 3 or 4.000 Deutschmark. So it turned out to be virtually impossible or very few people could afford to leave. Then Amir Delic and I agreed once again to go yet again. We asked the gentleman who took us there for the first time to drive us there again. He took us there the same way he did the first time and then we came to the hotel once again. However, they were very brief, they said that they could not do anything for us, that they did not have that kind of mandate, or, rather, a mandate that would include that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that therefore we should go to -- well, to the international police force in Dvor that was at a different locality, that we should go and talk to them. To see whether they could do anything by way of helping us. Because we were asking the presence of the United Nations, we wanted them to be with us, we wanted to know what would happen on the way out, we wanted them to protect us from possible attacks which might occur on the road. When we arrived there was a gentleman, I think that he was a captain, he very briefly told us that he could do nothing for us, that that was not his mandate and that we could leave. We didn't even enter the compound where he was. He greeted us at the entrance. We were disappointed. We returned to Bosanski Novi. And when the neighbours came to see what's new, we told them that probably something would happen but we really couldn't say what. We felt that nothing much would come of that particular situation. However, after only a couple of days, a vehicle with UNPROFOR markings stopped in front of my house and Mr. Jens and then this gentleman, Mr. Drazic, whom I mentioned, they were probably there, I am not sure but I think they probably went to the municipality and asked somebody to bring them to my house and they came to my house. They asked if they could come in so that we could talk, and I said yes, of course, that's what I want as well. Of course, they could come in. But I also invited Amir Delic and Azemir Ceric to take part in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that a conversation only with those persons you mentioned or were there already -- or were there any persons involved from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any contact with people from the Crisis Staff other than the people on the bridge. And there is a tape. This actually -- this shot is from that tape. The people who were on that cassette, there are some others who are not shown on this photograph, also talked about that. As for other conversations, I'm sorry but it can easily be that I have forgotten some details after so much time has passed, or some events. What I said, though, I remember well, and all that I have said is true. Maybe some details have now faded from memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you talked on the bridge with the people we see at the photograph, what was the position taken by Mr. Pasic, who was in the Crisis Staff, I take it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: What was their position? We knew each other very well. I knew Mr. Pasic. We worked together. I knew -- I know his character. At the time, he seemed to be a changed person. He talked in a very authoritarian manner, and I remember well that when we talked about -- I'm going to go back a little bit. Mr. Jens said that he wanted the people to stay in Bosanski Novi. He wanted to avoid people from moving out and that the international community would help with food. And that people should stay there. And he said, I remember that very well, "No, they cannot stay here." And you could sense that the whole atmosphere was that they wanted us to go, to leave, which suited us as well, I must admit, because had it not been for that will, it would have been difficult for us to get organised and to leave that chaos behind. I also wanted to add that the same will was there on the behalf of the police and Mr. Nikola, the commander from Dvor. I forgot his last name. Nikola is his first name. He also indicated that he would do everything he could so that the convoy, and we are already talking about the convoy now, would leave Bosanski Novi and cross the territories of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it during the conversation on the bridge, one of these conversations, that Mr. Jens said that he wanted you to say, people to stay in Bosanski Novi? Did he directly say that to those present?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: He said that also the first time at my house. And then again he said it on the bridge, and each time we spoke, he would mention this question and he wanted some compromise to be found so that people could stay. And I think that we took this as a negative thing on his part because in that way he was preventing us from leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he explain why he preferred you to stay?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: He said this, as far as I can remember. "We are here to prevent ethnic cleansing and not to aid it." These are the words that I recall. And we want these people to stay in their homes and on their hearths. This was something that was a feature of practically every conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that you wanted to leave due to the circumstances you found yourselves in. Could I first ask you, you're talking about I think you said people detained in the stadium, or at least you said something about the stadium. Could you tell us what stadium or which stadium?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: That's the stadium of the Sloboda football club, which is some 500 to 600 metres out of town in the direction of Bosanska Krupa, near the Una River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have heard a name Mlakve stadium. Is that the same stadium?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the same stadium, because earlier, before the stadium was built, that area was called Mlakve. Then when the stadium was built, because the old one was actually located in town, but it was called the Sloboda stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were you detained there at any time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see people being detained in the Mlakve stadium yourself? Did you observe them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, I really didn't dare go there. I didn't dare venture out of my house. When the camp was set up, none of the men dared to go towards the stadium because it could easily have happened that they would get caught, those who were not arrested already and at the stadium were very careful not to move around on the streets in case they ended up at the stadium. But I know that food was being sent, some women, some young women were brave enough, and they took food, cigarettes, socks. We were sending clothes also. Those women would take those things to the stadium and then they would ask the guards to hand the items over to the people that the items were actually sent to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take you back in a more general way to the events in Bosanski Novi at the time? Do you remember, when the first -- when you first experience any violence in your municipality, violence of a more -- so I'm not single shot but how did the conflict start in the municipality but, first of all, when did it start?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: The beginning could be traced back to maybe early April. The HOS until its perhaps began to be noticed after the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Already at that time you could sense in the enterprises, factories, that there were divisions amongst workers, but this was not of a major scale. However, every day these confrontations would become more pronounced. The enterprises where the managers were Serbs and they were mostly Serbs, began to illegally dismiss people from work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there? My question, but perhaps I was not clear enough to you, my question was mainly aiming at any violence by the use of arms. Could you tell us when the conflict in that respect started?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, I could say that this was no conflict. As far as a conflict is concerned, to have a conflict you need to have two parties, two sides, and both had weapons. The Muslims, however, didn't have weapons. I'll tell you that when the whole neighbourhood of Urije was searched and it's a mostly Muslim inhabited neighbourhood, that day they ordered that every one there should move out of their houses and they were brought to one place in Urije so that about 500 people who had been expelled from their homes were escorted by soldiers and military vehicles, the soldiers wore JNA uniforms, so with this escort they were taken to the school. And they also bore a white sheet on a long pole. I don't know why they had to use this white sheet as a sign of surrender because nobody ever took part in any fighting. When they did the search -- yes, actually, let me go back to something. When we informed the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you first? Do you remember when that happened? You were talking about events in Urije? Could you locate that in time? If you can, please do so. If you can't, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: This was maybe on the 10th or the 11th of May, approximately at that time. And everyone was told to bring their weapons, if they had one, they were to bring it with them. If they had a licence for the weapon or if it was an illegal weapon, they were to bring it any way. So all those who had a weapon brought it with them. There were some pistols, hunting rifles, and all of that was placed on a piece of tarpaulin where they were all gathering, and a certain man called Dejanovic was taking these weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there? Did you see that by yourself?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see that myself. All these people were brought to the school which is next to my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us which school that is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: This is the high school centre, the gymnasium and also vocational training school because there is another school centre in individual ora. Next to that school sent they are is a handball court. It has its own courtyard. So that's where the people were brought on that day. All of them were brought there. Nobody was allowed to remain in their homes, not even the youngest children, babies, newborns, women, the elderly, the infirm, all were brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once they were brought into the school what then happened to them? Did they have to stay there? Could they leave the school again? Could you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: They stayed there for two days and two nights. But may I expand on this? On that same day, I think it was the same day, a group from a different neighbourhood, which is called Prekosanje -- I'm not sure, I do apologise. The first neighbourhood I referred to as Urije. And the neighbourhood of Prekosanje had the same fate. It's on the other side of the railroad. They were given the same kind of orders, that they should all gather at the railway station, that she should all come to the railway station, no exceptions, and then all together there they set out in a column, again with these white sheets on long poles. They had a military escort and these people were actually keeping them at gunpoint, these military escorts were. My -- and then they were taken to the school. My house is right next door to the school and of course I was present when they were brought in. We actually established contact with them then. We gave them food, we took milk for the children. We gave them whatever we could. They stayed there for two days and two nights, I think. They were told that they were not allowed to leave unless specifically given permission for that. In the meantime, all the houses were searched, in detail. After that, they were told that they could go back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You used rather strong words when you said that you all wanted to leave. Could you tell us because until now I see that people were, houses were searched, they were taken to a school, they had to stay there for two days and were allowed to return home. Could you perhaps first indicate briefly what the kinds of events were that made you decide that the situation was too bad to stay?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? When 10.000 people believe that it is their lucky day when they are leaving their homes and everything, then I had to consider myself to be lucky too, to leave that hell. Now I'm going to tell you about it in greater detail. Many of my friends, intellectuals and those who were not intellectuals, were taken away for no reason whatsoever to a hotel. Some people were taken to the fire brigade building. Others to the police station. They were beaten up there, interrogated. People who were sick, even people who were disabled were treated the same way. Some managed to get out by paying money for it. Dzafer Kapetanovic, a good friend of mine, Resad Berberovic, another good friend of mine, were all taken away. A good friend of mine, Imo, right this moment I cannot recall his last name, they were all taken away and I never saw them again. They were just members of the SDA party. If I were to tell you that during a single night in Prekosanje this neighbourhood I mentioned that's next to the railway station, on one particular morning, 12 or 11 Muslims, Bosniaks, were killed and one Serb, and that Serb was killed because he tried to protect his neighbours. He said, "Stop, people. These are nice people. They are good people. Don't do anything to them. They are not to be blamed for anything." That's why they killed him too. So they were killed randomly there. I can tell you that there were lists of people who were supposed to be taken away. And now that you asked me about my personal view, as to whether I personally felt this, in terms of why I wanted to leave, one evening, at dusk, we heard the door of my house. When you open the door, rather the gate, you hear the iron gate opening. I had a little dog, a Pekingese dog and he reacted immediately. He started barking and I said to my wife, go and see who is at the door. She went to the door and she saw three soldiers and she said, "Run. They are coming to get you." I jumped out of the window then, and I fled through some gardens, hid behind some houses. They asked that I report to them so that they would take me to this hotel for an interview. However, I didn't want to show up. They said that I should come and that they would be back within half an hour. In the meantime, my wife got in touch with a gentleman I already mentioned, Mr. Drazic. She said they've come to get my husband. Do you know anything about it? He said that he had no idea what was going on and that it would be better for me not to show up and not to report to them. They waited for a while, my wife was talking to them and women from the neighbourhood gathered there as well. As a matter of fact, these people had other people who were issuing orders to them. They were bringing certain people in and then they would ask either for money or for some other reasons they were dealing with people, and for those other reasons people lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- a few short questions. You said they asked that I report to them. To whom did they ask for you to report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to go to the hotel. That's where the military police was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was not clear, I think. To whom did they say that you would have to report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: That's what they said to my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. You said, as a matter of fact, these people had other people who were issuing orders to them. What makes you say this?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, these men who came to get me were very young men. They didn't know me. I didn't know them. They didn't know who I was and they didn't know what benefit it would be to them if they were to take me away. They received these instructions from somebody who knew that I was a businessman and they probably thought that I had some valuables and they wanted to get their hands on that. That's what they did to other people too. I know for sure that these men did not know me because when they came, they same is this Emin Puric's house? And when my wife said, "yes," then they said that I was supposed to come with them. So these people themselves did not know me. They were sent by someone else who knew me very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Was any -- were any arms used by Muslims against Serbs in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that there was no organised resistance and not even unorganised resistance. Not a single shot was fired by the Muslims from the very beginning. Or, rather, from the moment when the tensions started, if I can put it that way. On the radio, they would say that all of a sudden the Green Berets appeared, and that they were warning the population that the Green Berets are somewhere out there and that they should be reported. Green Berets, that meant that those were the Muslim forces. However, no Green Berets were ever caught, dead or alive. No one ever fired a gun at all. Even if there was some shooting, all of that had been staged. There were people who saw Serbs shooting -- I mean people we knew, our acquaintances. They would shoot at the neighbourhood of Prekosanje, and over the radio they would say that it was the green berets that were shooting from Kula and so on and so forth. So it was insinuations of that kind. And deceptions of that kind so it was quite clear to us what this was all about. Also, no weapons were found during all the house searches, apart from hunting weapons or trophy weapons or small pistols and things like that. Practically all houses were searched in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of events which took place in the Japra Valley, in the Bosanski Novi municipality?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know about things at the actual moment when they were happening. I heard about things only when we joined the convoy, when I was leaving Bosanski Novi for Karlovac with these people who had suffered. I talked to many of these people because I knew of their suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there? Do I correctly understand that when you talk about the convoy, that the convoy included people who came from the Japra Valley?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that convoy left for Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: This was on the 23rd of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were the people from what you heard from the Japra Valley escorted or transported right away from the Japra Valley to the convoy which left for Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then when -- perhaps you first tell us what you heard from them about what had happened in the Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: There was an even larger exodus than the one of the population from the town. Their tragedy began already in April when it was relatively quiet in the town. They were the -- first, actually, all the villages in the Japra Valley, which is about 18 kilometres long, there are seven to eight Muslim villages there, and in mid-April, approximately, the soldiers came and they expelled all the people from the houses, village by village. After that they searched the homes and the farms, looking for weapons. Once the entire village was searched, then they would bring them back. This happened with all the villages. And these are the villages of Gornji Agici, Dedici, Hozici, Maslovare, Crna Rijeka, and finally Blagaj, which is at the entrance of the Japra Valley and it's the largest village. And this village of Blagaj and all the other villages, were emptied by the -- and persecuted by the soldiers. So that was the first violent act undertaken by the authorities. The next violent act took place on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that violence consisted of what?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: The next act was that on that date. I can't remember the exact date. It was actually between the 15th and the 20th of May sometime, all the villages that I mentioned in the Japra Valley, starting from Gornji Agici, Dedici, and so on and so forth, I already mentioned them, the people of those villages were ordered that they had to leave their homes. People who had tractors or horse carts loaded their belongings on those and those who didn't have any vehicles went on foot, and they came to the first village next to the Sana river, the village of Blagaj. That was the largest village. All of the population was assembled in that village. And they were there for about 15 or 20 days, until about the 10th of June. I can't remember the precise dates but it's approximately around that time. So they were all forced into that one village and they never returned to their homes after that. After they moved out, for several days, looting went on, the livestock, the property from those villages was looted, and then after that, every single house in the villages was burned, maybe two or three houses remained intact. I know that after the war, I went there and I saw that everything had been burned to the ground. People said that about some 9.000 heads of livestock stayed behind and all of them were gathered together, there was robbing and looting for a few days and then after that everything was set on fire. In one of the villages, the village of Maslovare some families, Ekic and Alic families, numbering some 27 people, stayed behind, and with their Serb neighbour who said that he would protect them because he was on good terms with them, and so they thought that he would be able to protect them and they decided to stay. However, after a few days, I can't say exactly how many days, all the families were killed, down to the last member. If I can just finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you -- since this is not a -- your -- the knowledge obtained by yourself, but since it's hearsay, please finish. The Chamber would not be greatly assisted to hear many details of matters which you have not experienced yourself and on which the Chamber received already some evidence from other sources. But please finish. Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just say that this information that I got from people who were with me there, after the war, when the grave was found, and only five and a half bodies were found in that grave instead of 27. So the question is what happened to that mass grave? I want to finish with this part about what happened to these people after they came to Blagaj. They were there until approximately the 9th of June and then on the 9th of June -- I'm not sure whether it was the 9th or the 10th of June; anyway, they were ordered, all, to leave Blagaj by crossing the bridge over the Sana river. All the tractors and the other vehicles that they had brought with them remained in the village of Blagaj and they started to walk across the bridge in a column. Soldiers were waiting on the bridge. There was a piece of tent canvass placed on the bridge. I wasn't there but when I was in Karlovac with some of these people they told me about these events. They -- not one person but several people told me about this. So there was a piece of tent canvass or placed or stretched across the bridge. They were told to place all of their valuables and their identity cards and papers on this piece of canvass. They were also told that they would not be needing their identification documents any more. This upset people because they could guess what that meant. On that day, on the bridge, and around the bridge, it was said that 17 people were killed on that day. Some names were mentioned. I know some of the people that were mentioned and I know that they were killed. When they all crossed the bridge, they were all forced to go to the compound of the Japra mine. There is a fenced-in plateau that belongs to the mine and that's where they were all assembled. It didn't matter what their age was. The youngest child and the oldest man or woman, the sick, were all taken there. After that, sometime in the evening, a train came comprising of cattle cars and they were ordered to get into those cars. I was told that a paralysed woman was brought in a wheelbarrow and put into one of those cars. I don't know how true that is but I do trust that man. So children starting from one year old and all the other people were placed in these train cars. When the railcars were filled, the car -- the train set off towards Banja Luka and Doboj. It was stopped at the Stanari railway station. They arrived there sometime in the morning and they waited there until about noon. Then they were told to leave the rail cars and that militarily-fit men would -- should go to one side and all the other people should go to the other. When this division was made, the men were returned to the railcars and the others, women and children, were sent to the line of division or line of separation, towards Gracanica; the line of separation with the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tell us what happened to the men? Where did they end up?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: They boarded the train, and I was told that the cars were so full that they didn't have enough air. They said that there were as many as 180 people. I mean people knew this. And with their bear hands, they managed to pull away a few slats of the rail wall to get some air. They did this with their bare hands. They wouldn't let them go to the toilet or anything like that and it was suffocating. So throughout that whole time, from the time when they left Blagaj -- may I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, this Chamber has received evidence from other sources and would like to hear from you what -- approximately was what you heard from the people you spoke with at a later stage. So my question was where did -- what happened to the men? Where did they finally end up, the men?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I was just getting to that part when their fate was being decided. When they returned, they went to Blagaj, that's what they told me and they were kept there for a while until the evening. Then in the evening that same train took them to the stadium because the railway tracks passed towards Krupa and Bihac and they passed by the stadium. So that was when they were taken off the train and taken straight to the stadium, escorted by soldiers. So practically they left the rail cars and entered the stadium which is very close to the railway tracks. Then, this is what I was told, that was the first time that they received food. This was on the 9th of June or the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now take you back briefly again to the negotiations. When you had these meetings, as you said, two meetings on the bridge, first of all, were you aware of any people staying at that moment, if it was at that moment, in the Mlakve stadium?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that, and I said something about that the first time I went to Dvor, to the UNPROFOR staff. They said they knew about the existence of that, that they were monitoring and observing that location. We knew about that the whole time. And if I may add, when we were talking with these representatives, I mean with Mr. Pasic, we asked -- I did and the people that you see here, we said that we would not leave unless the people from the stadium were released as well. We didn't want to leave unless all the people were released from the stadium as well. And they said that they would be released. However, when we set off the first time -- I have to inform this Trial Chamber that the first time we attempted to leave was not successful. We had two tries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber heard evidence about that so you don't have to go into -- you don't have to go into further details as far as the Chamber is concerned. So you said the first time -- you said they said that they would be released and then you continued, however, when we set off the first time, and then you started explaining about the first time and the second time. What did you experience at the first time in relation to the people of which you said that you would not leave unless they would be released?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I don't know where exactly I was unclear. The people who were at the stadium, we would send food to them and some other items that we were able to send them. Mainly the women would take these things to them. Many were up there, not only from the Japra Valley but also from the town of Bosanski Novi. We were in touch with them. They knew that there was a convoy being prepared. We knew that and they knew that the town was about to be evacuated so they were afraid that the convoy might leave without them. Everything was known, although we only talked about this on the bridge. And when we did talk about this on the bridge, there were several options suggested for our direction of movement. We wanted us first of all to leave towards Bihac or we wanted to go in the direction of Croatia. They, the authorities of Bosanski Novi, said that it was out of the question for us to go in the direction of Bihac, but that there was an option that we could go towards Travnik or towards Zagreb. Knowing that it would be very dangerous for us to go in the direction of Travnik we said that we didn't wish to go in the direction of Travnik but that we categorically requested to go in the direction of Croatia, to Croatia. I also insisted, as well as my colleagues who were there with me, that if we were to leave and if the people from the camp did not go with us, we simply would not continue with the journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Even when I'm not asking you in some respects about details, that's also due to time constraints and again, as I said before, this Chamber has received evidence from some other sources as well. Could you tell us, the activity, both from what you heard in the city and around and from what you observed yourself, you said young men asked your wife that you should report, this Chamber received evidence that these were uncontrolled paramilitaries who were active in the area. Is that something you could understand from your own observations at the time or would you like to comment on paramilitaries out of control being blamed for what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was quite important for us. And during the initial contacts with Mr. Jens, when Mr. Drazic from the municipality came to my house, this was discussed. When Mr. Jens asked that the authorities impose order and improve the security situation and prevent those who were committing these murders and so on, Mr. Drazic said that this was not done by the regulars or the Territorial Defence, as he said, but that this was done by groups who had -- who were no longer under anyone's control. I said that this was not true, and that this could very easily be resolved if there was goodwill to do that. Then Mr. Jens said, "How could this be done?" I said we could deal with this very simply if we were to set up mixed or joint guards because at the time you had different guards duties at the entrances to the villages, junctures and so on but they were exclusively Serb people in those guards. And I just said, well, let's make mixed or joint guards and then they would receive weapons and then each side could deal with their own people if she should come up and this could be done very easily. However, Mr. Drazic said that this could not be done, that this cannot be prevented, these groups were out of control and it wasn't possible to do anything about it but I think that that wasn't true. The Crisis Staff knew who was doing what. They knew everything by name. They knew about people being taken away, people getting killed and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say I think that that wasn't true and then you give your impression. You said the Crisis Staff knew. How do you -- on the basis of what do you conclude that the Crisis Staff knew?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in contact with them. So I really couldn't get that on the basis of a conversation. I didn't even want to be in contact with them. But if I may digress briefly before I say more, there was an offer by the Crisis Staff made over the radio for Muslim intellectuals to get organised and to form a negotiation group so that weapons could be handed over and so that the Green Berets would be prevented from operating. I and none of the others either wished to even consider something like that, to form a negotiating team for something that didn't even exist, to settle the matter of resistance that didn't even exist, because the Muslims were not putting up any resistance, with or without weapons, so that it would have been a pointless game for us to be looking for some Green Berets that were not there at all and to be negotiating, but there were no Green Berets at all and we said we didn't even want to negotiate about that. If you think that we had weapons, then you conducted searches so you worked out if we have weapons or not. So all the moves, not only theirs but our moves as well, were something that was widely known, what we were trying to do in order to leave and so on. It was all known to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question about the negotiations on the bridge. You asked permission to leave, and I do understand that it was more than fully supported, that it was even required that you should leave. Did you ever raise the issue of returning to your own places, the places where you lived? Was that ever a subject discussed during these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: You mean negotiations before we left in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No. It was pointless to even mention this to them. It was a question that had no sense at all at that point. We wanted to leave, to save our lives, but now I'm going to tell you what we felt as we were leaving. When the convoy was leaving, journalists came and they put questions to certain people about that. What they felt at that moment and so on. And that was on the tape. A journalist came and he asked the same question of me, and I was very careful of what I was going to say, and I said what I felt at that moment, and that was that I was happy that I can leave at this time but that I hoped that after a while, we would be able to live together again in this area. This is what I thought and this is what everyone else thought. But at that moment, there was even no possibility of us being able to come back at some time in the future. I have some documents and if you don't have those documents, I can show them to you. They were documents saying that we were voluntarily and permanently moving out. We needed to fill in all of these things, these forms, because they said in order for you to leave you have to get some documents, and that is the certificate of no previous criminal record, that you had served your regular military duty, that you were giving up your property, and that you are voluntarily and permanently leaving your homes. These were the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give up your property or did you exchange or sell your property? Could you -- just a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly. I gave away my property to my brother-in-law who stayed in my house. His house was actually burned. He didn't leave because his wife happened to be a Serb, so his son came with me, his older son, and the younger son stayed with him, with his parents, so he gave my house away to my brother-in-law. And if I may add something, those prisoners, when they were leaving the stadium, that day or the day before, they all had to sign a piece of paper saying that they were leaving their property either to somebody or to the municipality; every single one had to sign such a paper. I wasn't there but this is what they told me, "We all had to sign a paper saying that we were giving up or giving our property away."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you saw these men on the streets, these guards, these soldiers. You've talked about. And you also said that you saw them very close to your house. You saw them also while you were having your negotiations, but also you said that these men intervened in the Japra Valley. Who were they, according to you? Who were these men? Who were these armed men? Where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: You know how these armies functioned in our part of the world? Usually we were taken away by unknown soldiers. We now say that they came from Croatia from Dvor, then they came from a different town in Bosnia itself, from Kostajnica, from villages. The local Serbs distanced themselves from that. Well, not always. Sometimes some of them did not hesitate to join in. But for the most part, they were some kind of military that came from another area. The same went for the Japra Valley. It's not that -- I mean, you didn't know those people so you could not really make any requests to them. Even if you knew them personally, they were so disciplined -- well, sometimes they would give someone in the stadium a cigarette or somebody would bring food in to the stadium, but as for some closeness with these people, the kind of closeness we had before, it was no longer there. I cannot understand the kind of discipline that existed then, that these people whom I had known could change to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding these men that you knew, that you knew up until that time, did they also become soldiers? Did they also become soldiers and were they also against you in a way? Soldiers fighting you or did they remain civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No. All joined in, very gladly, if I can put it that way. My colleagues from work took part in this, in this military activity. A young man, whose name is Mladen Krnjajic, I was his superior at work. As a matter of fact, I took him in for that job, and then when I came for those negotiations on that day, when Drazic was supposed to receive us, he, as commander of town, happened to be there. I was flabbergasted. He had the rank of major or something like that. We said hello to each other but he was very official in the way he spoke to me. In all fairness he said, no problem, go ahead. But I didn't notice any embarrassment or anything when we came across each other. I know of a lot of other cases of people I worked with who put uniforms on and carried out the assignments they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, the Chamber has no further questions but after the break, which we'll have now, the parties will have an opportunity to put further questions to you. Mr. Tieger, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would think 15 to 20 minutes at the most. I'm going to discuss that during the break but it may be that there is even less time required. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would then the -- Mr. Stewart or Mr. Josse, the remainder of that session, the president was a bit longer but let's just assume that the second session would then be approximately one hour and 20 minutes instead of the usual one hour and 30 minutes. Would the remaining hour do for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will make sure that it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then of course it was announced that there would be another filing for which a courtesy copy is to be sent to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been filed because during this session it's come through on to my system as an official filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not a bad idea that we start reading already. We adjourn until five minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I wish to inform the Chamber and Mr. Puric that I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions for Mr. Puric. That's very brief. Counsel for the Prosecution has no questions for you, Mr. Puric. Mr. Josse, that means that I give an opportunity to you now to put questions to Mr. Puric. Mr. Puric, Mr. Josse is counsel for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Towards the end of the questions asked by the learned Presiding Judge, you were asked whether you can recall any discussion in the negotiations about the possibility of your return to Bosanski Novi when things became safer, quieter, the war ended, or whatever. Do you remember that question, Mr. Puric?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as I understood your answer, it was that at no point in the negotiations was the issue of the return of any Bosniaks to the municipality discussed. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure about that. During the course of the negotiations, we never mentioned that we intended to return. As a matter of fact, we did not even dare discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did anyone else mention it, be it any Serb or international negotiator or anyone else? Was this subject ever discussed or mentioned in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: The Serbs never mentioned that. I think the members of the international community who took part in the negotiations also did not discuss that, or rather they did not mention any return to that area. I mean, directly, that somebody was saying, all right, you'll return within a certain period of time. No. That was not mentioned. At that moment, we did not insist on talking about any return at all, although we knew and hoped for a time when we would come back because I knew that what was going on then had to be brought to an end and that ultimately we would go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll return, if I may, Mr. Puric, to that subject in a few minutes' time. You have made some reference to a film that was made at the time of some of the events that you have described. That's right, isn't it? Such a film is in existence?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There is a cassette that was recorded by journalists. I was aware of the fact that these negotiations were being recorded at the time, but I got that cassette much later, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I don't want to mislead you in any way at all. Mr. Delic, when he came to this Chamber, provided the parties with copies of that video. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the same cassette that I have and that he has. We both have that cassette. I have that cassette at home too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question is, did you know that Mr. Delic had provided a copy to the Chamber for it to consider? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And digressing if I may nor a moment, were you able to follow Mr. Delic's evidence? Did you watch it on the internet or any such medium?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No. I did not follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So how do you know that Mr. Delic provided the video to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well I knew Mr. Delic was invited and he's my neighbour. My house and his father's house are right next door. We saw each other. I knew that he was going to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That doesn't entirely answer my question. How precisely did you know that he had provided the video to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: He told me. He told me that he handed over his cassette. I wanted to bring that same cassette along and I asked him whether it was necessary for me to bring it here but then I said, if you brought your cassette there, then there is no need for me to take mine. And he said that he had shown his cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What else did he tell you about his evidence or his experiences in The Hague in general?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: He didn't exactly talk to me about his evidence, what he concretely spoke of. After he arrived, we talked a bit, I was interested in what this looked like, what the procedure was, and so on and so forth. At the time, when this cassette was being created and when our trips were being organised, we were together all the time. We were always in touch. We talked about this together, with people from the international community and people from the municipality. During the course of these conversations, we were together every day so we knew what was going on. He didn't particularly tell me about his evidence, what he stated, nothing special. I was sort of interested in the procedure, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Returning if I may to the video, when was the last time you watched it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I watched it often. The last time I watched it was only a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that it shows between 15 and 30 minutes, you, Mr. Pasic, Mr. Delic, the two officers from the Krajina, and Mr. Jens above all else, negotiating?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that the first or the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I think this was the first meeting, what you can see on the cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that among the things that Mr. Jens asks Mr. Pasic is whether there was -- whether the Bosnian Serb authorities in the municipality were prepared to guarantee the return of the Bosniak community in the event of the situation in the area improving?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit more about the video. We can see on the video quite a number of people milling around in the background. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I identified some of the people that were there. A lot of people who were there -- or rather some people came from Republika Srpska Krajina, they stopped. It wasn't that there were some people who started the negotiations and who stayed on there. Many Muslims or rather some Muslims who were there joined in later, because they knew me, Delic and some other people, they joined in because they knew that negotiations were under way and they wanted to take part in these negotiations in order to contribute to having this problem resolved. So there were some people who just happened to come and then they joined in. Delic and I were practically in all the negotiations. We were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know the nationality and the ethnicity of the cameraman?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I think that he's an ethnic Serb. He was filming for TV Novi Sad. I don't know if that is the origin but I don't think that there was anyone else there but him and he's from Novi. He's from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful because that leads to my next question which was or which is whose idea was it to create this historical contemporaneous record of these rather important negotiations?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm the last person you should ask that question, because at that time we could not have any influence over anyone, in terms of filming or not filming. We could not forbid it, we could not ask someone to do it. It was of their own volition. They wanted to film this and that TV was watched in the area of Bosanski Novi, or rather it was TV Belgrade that was watched the most at that time. So it was Novi Sad and Belgrade. He was the correspondent of TV Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So it was very much a Serb production, this film, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you know - and only say if you can help - when and where the film was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I never saw that on TV. At that time, when we were negotiating and so on and so forth, it would have been ridiculous for us to watch it and to follow the news. We were in basements most of the time. After we got out, we could not watch that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you get your copy of the programme?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I got this copy from a person from Bihac. Now, how that person happened to get that copy, I have no idea. But that person originally comes from Bosanski Novi and this person called me and then this person said that this was filmed on that cassette when we left and I asked if I could get a copy. They made a copy and that's how I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the film has ever been broadcast on terrestrial television, either in Bosnia, Serbia, or indeed anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I know. And I'll tell you now how come. When I came to Zagreb after the convoy left, a month or two later I met a lady I knew before the war. We happened to see each other on the tram and she told me that she had seen me on television, making a statement when the convoy was about to leave. I did not watch that TV programme but she told me about this and I know, therefore, that it had been broadcast. Now, when that took place, I don't know, and I told you that I could not have watched it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind you saw it recently, you may be able to help in a number of regards. It starts, does it not, with an interview with Mr. Pasic which lasts for about five minutes, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that. I recall that. I mean, the footage that you saw are excerpts from the overall conversation. The beginning of this cassette is not the actual beginning of the discussion, I think. These discussions went on a lot longer than what you can see on the cassette. So these are excerpts and there are interruptions too. So these discussions went on much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you misunderstood me. What I'm suggesting to you is certainly on the film that we have been provided with, it begins with an interview, not part of the negotiation, an interview with Mr. Pasic, presumably by a journalist. Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: If that's the part at the bridge, if that interview took place on the bridge, the one with Mr. Pasic, then I was there. If it was not on the bridge, then I wasn't there. I know very well that I was not present during any interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, I'm not suggesting for one moment you were there. I'm just simply asking whether you had seen this interview with Pasic on the film. If you can't remember, say so. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Your question is not very clear. That interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. After the 20- to 30-minute extract of the negotiation on the bridge, there is an interview -- I beg your pardon. You're seen on the video, I suggest, talking to a soldier from the United Nations. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. I remember that full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was that about, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: That took place when the convoy had already been put in place, and was ready to leave. There was a bus in the first place in the convoy, and then there were these other buses and behind all the buses there were passenger vehicles. The convoy was not leaving at all, so I left my own personal vehicle there and I came to the head of the column and I asked the representatives of the international community to let us go. These talks actually took place because the representative of the international community did not allow the convoy to leave, to reach the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, as he called it. You heard what the reason was, why they were not allowing us to go. That was stated very clearly during that conversation. You could have heard that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
