utterances.text: Unfortunately, and I'm not here to give evidence, but I've clearly viewed it and the questions I'm asking -- as I see the situation, though you were talking to that soldier through an interpreter, the soldier was not speaking English. The soldier came from a non-English speaking country and the translator was translating through the soldier's language so I'm afraid I didn't understand that passage at all. Just for your information. You understand, I only understand English and that conversation was not conducted in English at all. Perhaps you can tell us, do you know which country that soldier came from?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to speak with any high degree of certainty but I think it was the Danish battalion and the representative was from Denmark. I have with me a note that this gentleman who I negotiated with gave me so that I could use it as a pass in a way so that we go from Kostajnica, Dubica, Draksevic, Jasenovac so that we move along the Bosnian side and that's ultimately what we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst the witness is finding that, this isn't meant to be some secret tour -- one moment, please -- which we are trying to deprive the Chamber from being part of. In fact the Defence would very much encourage the Chamber to have an opportunity to view the whole of this video. It's about an hour long. The Chamber has expressed an interest, understandably, in these negotiations as you've heard from the witness. I don't need to give evidence about this. The video depicts 20 to 30 minutes of negotiation on the bridge. There are practical problems in producing this video for the Chamber. There is absolutely no prospect in the Defence providing a transcript. None whatsoever, frankly, Your Honour. It would take far too long but there are -- the whole of the video, Chamber, I would venture to suggest, would find interesting. Perhaps it's something we could address when the witness is finished but I just want the Chamber to be aware that this examination is not designed as some sort of a device to put the video in without the Court having an opportunity to see it. Quite the reverse. We would welcome the Chamber to view it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but I also do understand I take it then that it's subtitled or translated voiceover but where the witness says --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, no, no. May I just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The negotiations on the bridge, Mr. Jens speaks English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the passage you just referred to where this witness is speaking to a soldier who seems to speak another language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where this witness says you could have heard what he said. So I take it in one way or the other either by subtitling or by voice over at least it's translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is a translator translating it for the benefit of Mr. Puric at the time in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine, that's not translated into English. But if Mr. Puric says you could have heard what his position was why he opposed, why not ask him at this moment because Mr. Puric seems to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not against that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Puric, as you may have understood from Mr. Josse, the words spoken by the soldier, you thought, was Danish but that's not most important, that he could not follow it because it's not translated into English. Could you tell us what the words of this Danish soldier were as it was translated to you at the time? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our conversation was basically that they were trying to persuade us or rather to persuade me that it was impossible for the convoy to go in the direction that we wanted to go in and that they did not have clearance for letting us go that way. I said something then, I said that we as refugees have certain rights, and that they cannot deny us those rights. I believed then that our rights were the following: That we had the right to seek protection by entering the territory of another state. I'm an economist, I knew just a bit of law so I availed myself of that opportunity to say that particular thing. We, however, were being persuaded that there was no possibility for us to set foot on the territory of the Republic of Croatia or the then Republic of Serb Krajina and that they were there to prevent us from entering that area. He gave me a piece of paper that I've kept since. It's a sort of pass. He wrote here that we should take a different route, Bosanska Kostajnica, Bosanska Dubica, Draksevic, Jasenovac. That's the piece of paper. See? And it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually, Mr. Puric, you're not allowed to consult any piece of paper but you did it so openly, perhaps it could be put on the ELMO so that we could have a look at it and see whether there is any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's clearly an original document, Your Honour. It's not quite like a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm all for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and see whether -- yes. At least it gives the names of -- I leave it to the parties whether there is any need to have this as a supporting document of the evidence of the witness. I think you now told us what this soldier told you at the time. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what's that? Is that the soldier's signature at the bottom there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the soldier's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Though I'm basically neutral Your Honour it would make more sense on the transcript if the piece of paper was copied and exhibited, I would venture to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Puric, would you mind to give it for just a short while, because I take it that you'd like to keep the original. The original is now at least available for the parties to inspect if they want to. Then a copy will be made, the original will be returned to you, and would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's given to the representative of the Registry for copying. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could it have a number, then, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber's number might not be a bad idea. Chamber's number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: C9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the extract of your speaking to the Danish soldier, I'm sorry, I want to ask you a little bit more about that. It's obvious that the cameraman was following you and was filming your discussion with the Danish soldier. How comes the cameraman was following you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: If you can believe me, at that point in time, I wasn't even aware that it was being filmed. I didn't even know it was being filmed. Everything was focused on the conversation with that gentleman and on the problem that we were discussing. You could see that I was excited. I didn't even notice the cameraman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, at what point, if at all, did it strike you that this whole process showed a certain amount of openness by the Serbs in allowing this process to be filmed? If you don't agree with that proposition, say so. I don't want to put words into your mouth.

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Could you please reformulate your question, put it differently?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think that by allowing the negotiation on the bridge, your discussion with the Danish soldier, to be filmed, that this showed a certain openness on the part of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Openness or goodwill, I don't really see any openness or goodwill in relation to us. It's just a gesture indicating that they were not ashamed of that fact that people were leaving. They behaved as if it was some kind of sports event, that it was a normal event. For us, it was a matter of life and death. For them, it was a television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go on, bearing in mind the answer you've just given and look at -- examine what's on the rest of the video. After your conversation with the Danish soldier, there is an extract from a meeting in a room, a meeting that takes place round some sort of table. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting, and you don't see me on that tape. I didn't participate at the meeting and I don't know anything about it. It's a part of the tape that was recorded after it was broadcast on some Serbian programme. That segment of the tape was filmed after the attempt -- the events on the bridge. So it happened after that, and I wasn't present at that meeting so I don't know what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's helpful, but you have seen the extract, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I just went over that as if it had nothing to do with me. So many things there were so superficially edited in order to create the impression that this was some law and order there. It was a charade of legality, the return or restoration of robbed property. You can guess how much of the property was looted. Suddenly they showed one corner of one -- of the place where I was working, as that having been returned in order to try to create the impression that the rule of law was being enforced again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, Mr. Puric, that your remark that this film was superficially edited is an unfair one in the extreme because, in particular, if one looks at the extract of this round-table meeting, which I haven't yet described to the Chamber, there is no question that the international negotiator is being extremely condemnatory of the behaviour of the Serbs. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about that part that was in the offices or something like that, if you're asking me about that, then I really don't want to comment, that event or that discussion or that speech. Other than what was said on the bridge, that's the only thing that I can talk about. As far as all the rest, it's really something that I am not informed about. I didn't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question I asked a minute or two ago. Have you watched that extract of the film, the extract that depicts the round-table discussion inside a room?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I can say that when I looked at the tape again, I simply skipped those parts. I skipped that part of the video because I wasn't interested in that. Those talks that were conducted, I am informed about it, I know that there is that part of the tape as well but I'm not interested in that. At that time and now I was interested in other things, and that's the problem that we were discussing on the bridge. That was the only thing that I was interested in. As for the rest, there were such talks. I know that probably there was more than even what was taped and what is on that cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to labour this point, Mr. Puric, but are you seriously suggesting that you did not watch the extract that I am just asking you about, the negotiation in the room round the table? You didn't watch that at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please specify now, ever, because the witness told us that it was only a couple of days before he came to The Hague that -- I'd like to make sure that there is no misunderstanding about that. So if you're answering that question, Mr. Puric, whether you saw the whole of the tape, were you referring or would you please make clear to the Chamber whether you ever saw the whole of the tape or when reviewing the tape recently whether you then watched the whole of it or just portions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time I watched, I watched those -- actually those parts that had nothing to do with the part on the bridge, I just skipped over. I watched carefully only the part where I was, the event in which I participated. The other parts I didn't really watch or analyse in any particular way. I wasn't even paying attention to what was being said. All I saw was an image of some talks in some room so I just skipped over that. I wasn't interested in that. And I believe that that has nothing to do with my testimony. I didn't take part in those talks. And I couldn't contribute in any way and I didn't hear anything directly about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, if a witness says that he doesn't appear in a certain portion of a film it's very difference of course for him to say so if he hasn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm effectively, as we would say in England, bound by the answer the witness has given and I'm going to move on, save for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In a spirit of genuine inquiry, do you have any idea who the person in that room is who does all the talking? Mr. Jens is in there but he doesn't do the speaking. Another member of the international community gives a long and rather impassioned speech in English. Do you have any idea who that person is?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next extract, part of the video, is the interview with yourself that you mentioned when you were being questioned by the learned judges; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: When the Judges were asking me, I'm not sure what exactly you're asking me, which part are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the Judges were asking you questions, you volunteered to them that on the video there is an interview with you, and that's the next extract, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you told the Judges before the break, a little bit about that interview. Is there anything else that you would like to add as to what you said and why you said it in the course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: On the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut that short. I think, Mr. Puric, that Mr. Josse is referring to -- for example, the part of your testimony in which you said that in the interview you said that you -- I have to look it up -- that although you did not discuss return during the negotiations, that you did express yourself on it on wishing to once return during this interview. I think that's the interview Mr. Josse is drawing your attention to at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, could I just say Mr. Wijermars has this video on a CD. It's perhaps possible that he can forward to this extract. I appreciate I'm asking a lot of him. He and I had a brief discussion about this at the break so that the witness knows the point that I am referring to. It's about two-thirds of the way through the film, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he only looks at it might refresh his memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask for it to be played. It would be too much of a task I suspect for the interpreters, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wijermars were you able to find -- I take it a still of that portion of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, ideally or 30 seconds of it. It doesn't need to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If it's not possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at your screen, we see at this moment a -- I think Mr. Josse is referring to this portion of the film, Mr. Puric, where it seems that you're interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to, Mr. Puric. Let's break it down. Who is interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: This is a journalist. His name is Bera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was interviewing you because you were one of the Muslim negotiators presumably; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Because of that, but also it was an opportunity -- actually it was the time when we had already gathered in the convoy and we were waiting for the sign to move, and he asked me if I would like to say a few words. I tried to avoid doing this. However, he insisted that I should say something. Then I agreed to say something. And it's taped. You can go ahead and look at it. I have nothing against you seeing the tape and listening to what I said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you listen to this extract of the tape a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I must say that this part on the tape that I listened to actually is missing from there. I don't have that. But I do remember that interview. There is no need for me to go over it. I know that this conversation took place and I know more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you help us at all? Giving us any more detail?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I already said that the main thrust of the conversation was that unfortunately we had to leave our homes and that I hoped that when these hard times were over, we would be able to return to our homes and that we would live together again. That was more or less the sense of my speech. He didn't say anything. He just said thank you and then he moved on and he interviewed other people who were in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Last question about the film, if I may. It ends, does it not, with the cameraman showing the long queue of motorcars, obviously owned by Bosniaks, that formed part of a column, several kilometres long, that eventually left the municipality? Do you remember that part of the film?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Of course. I remember the column, the buses, the private cars. It was all taped. The column was several kilometres long, as it was passing. It was all on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my question to you is this, Mr. Puric: The depiction of that brings home to a viewer the humanitarian difficulties that you and your people faced at that time cannot be described as a bit of superficial editing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'd like you, you are referring to this passage now not nor the first time, to quote it then very precisely. I think the witness said in some respects. He didn't say that the whole of the film was poorly edited. It's certainly not what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you used the word "superficially edited," what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was edited in the sense of some kind of film editing. What I said was that those excerpts were just parts of the conversation, that they were taken and put together; the actual talks lasted for much longer. There was mutual persuasion and so on. So if you're thinking about the part that I said where there was an attempt to create an image of a lawful state, when they were showing the restoration or the return of looted property, what I meant was that this was a propaganda kind of material because it's ridiculous to just show a few things that had been returned while scores of railcars figuratively were not restored, they were robbed and looted. So that symbol that was shown on the television was just ridiculous, but it was taped and I think that that was a kind of wish there to create the impression that the law was functioning and that this was not a state of lawlessness, whereas in actual fact that's exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was a state of lawlessness is what you're saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last issue relates to the talks in your house, Mr. Puric. You told us that Mr. Jens was there. Were any Serbs present?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that a representative of the municipal assembly was there, Drazen Dragomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of visits that members of the international community played to the homes of Muslims in Bosanski Novi at about this time, where Serbs were not present, the purpose of those visits being to ascertain how anxious Muslims were to leave?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: I really would not be able to answer that question because I really don't know. I did hear that they went to see some people, they wanted to hear their opinions, but I don't know that for sure because I simply wasn't leaving the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And who did you hear from that they went to see some people?

utterances.speaker: EMIN PURIC
utterances.text: If I were to give you a name I could make a mistake. At that time, all the information about events that reached us were something that we shared with each other, from that circle. Those from other streets who would manage to come and this was dangerous, they would bring news, for example, you would need to leave this particular neighbourhood because there would be shelling that evening. I don't know who told me that, but you could hear, people were there, they were talking about something, so it's not really a question that is very important to me when we are talking about this attempt to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't intend to ask any further questions. In the presence of the witness and before he leaves could I make it clear on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik and indeed the Defence in general that we would have been anxious to put parts of this video directly to the witness. Logistically I take the view that would be near enough impossible, apart from having to find the right passage, it's untranslated save for the fact that parts of the negotiation are translated actually on the video. There is no transcript and, logistically, to specifically ask the witness about it in the way that I would like to, in the way I would envisage, is near enough impossible. However, we are going to invite the Chamber to in some way admit the video into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider your request, then, perhaps -- the Prosecution might having an idea of how appropriate that would be under the present circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'll perhaps briefly in due course develop the submission as to why we say it should be admitted. I don't need to do that in the presence of Mr. Puric. I've just made my position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Doesn't change the present situation, you would say. That's no questions to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just don't think there is any way around it, realistically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It seems to the Prosecution, Your Honour, that if Mr. Josse wants to play parts of the video to the witness, he can do that. There is nothing to preclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm delighted if I can sort it out. My client agrees with my learned friend. He's very anxious that I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not convinced yet that it makes -- I mean from what the Chamber heard, but perhaps -- Mr. Puric, do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind to take your earphones off for a second? The Chamber doesn't know what to expect and what purpose it would serve. I mean, there seems to be, among whether we look at the testimony of Mr. Pasic or of the other witnesses, there seems to be not a lot of contradiction that the Muslims during the negotiations very much insisted on having an opportunity or at least to leave the municipality. I think the main issue for the Chamber might be, and whether the circumstances were such that the words "voluntary" would need further interpretation on what exactly means "voluntary" under those circumstances. I don't know to what extent the video would assist us in interpreting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, we are slightly surprised by that, for this reason. The Chamber expressed a real interest in this aspect of the [indiscernible] and the negotiations and lo and behold, unbeknownst certainly to the Defence and I dare say the Prosecution, the first Chamber witness comes along, mentions a video, the Chamber understands and distributes that to the parties and we discover that 20 to 30 minutes of the very negotiation --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- that these two witnesses have been brought here to describe is shown in full in colour. So to speak. And in those circumstances, how the Chamber takes the view that it's of no real interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No real interest. Of course what the Chamber wanted to do is to, where some of the witnesses said that it was because of the horrible situation that they wanted to leave, and where other witnesses said that it was totally different, to hear the testimony of those who were involved in those negotiations, and from what I understand, there is not a lot of disagreement on what positions were taken during these negotiations whereas until now we had only the information from some participants in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I remain on behalf of the Defence slightly puzzled because it's never been in dispute, so I thought, that the situation that the Bosniak community faced in the municipality was intolerable. The reasons for its intolerability is a matter that's in dispute. We were also under the impression that there was some dispute as to the view the international community took of these matters. Whilst I accept that Mr. Kirudja wasn't present at the bridge, Mr. Jens was negotiating on his behalf, and we would say that some of the things that Mr. Jens says supports the Defence interpretation of frankly the United Nations' stance at the time. In addition to that, Your Honour specifically asked the question of the witness as to what, if anything, was said about return. Mr. Jens asks Pasic about that. Now, in truth, that part was slightly inaudible and I can't say, and I'm not here to give evidence, exactly what Pasic said at that juncture in time but in our submission, that's highly relevant, there is no question that Jens brings up the issue and there is no question that Pasic responds and in our submission, the Chamber surely wants to view the video and see exactly what was said and by the participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now if you would play the video now, what would be the questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The questions for the witness would then flow from the video and, for example, that extract I would be very anxious to play and ask him whether that refreshes his memory, what he has to say about that, what he has to say about Pasic's response, why he didn't say anything at the time. I might ask him why it was he couldn't remember that extract earlier. Things of that sort. But, Your Honour, Your Honour, let me make it plain, it's not showing it to the witness that's the be all and the end all. I've taken the witness through it because I was concerned that if I sought to introduce the video, I and the Defence might be criticised for not having given the witness an opportunity to deal with it in some way. But frankly, our primary concern is that the Chamber views it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- warts and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll consider that. So you say although you would have preferred and you would like to avoid any criticism of not having put portions of the video to the witness, that at least you think it important for the Chamber to have the transcript available and to view the video at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, the provision of a transcript is a difficult and thorny issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we have some practical problems there but we'll -- yes, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The video is quite long, Your Honour. It depends on what portion of the video Mr. Josse is talking about. If we're talking about the section on the bridge, and that's the portion he wants the Court to view because that's the portion Mr. Puric has personal knowledge of, then that's one issue. If Mr. Josse is trying to get into evidence the remaining part of the video that Mr. Puric has -- for which he has no knowledge, that's a separate issue. I'd like some clarification from Mr. Josse as to what portion of the video he's referring to that he wants the Chamber to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would invite the Chamber to view, clearly it would require a translation, the interview with Mr. Pasic the video commences with, the 20- to 30-minute extract on the bridge, most certainly, the conversation -- the third passage in my note is the conversation between this witness and the Danish soldier. The fourth passage is the round-table meeting that I have described. I am bound to say that I'm not particularly anxious for the Chamber to view that. It doesn't help the Defence case very much at all but I would have thought my learned friend might wish the Chamber to view it. The fifth passage is the coaches leaving, that's silent, and the sixth passage is the other interview with Mr. Puric the Chamber has seen a still photograph from. And then the last part of it, according to my note, is the convoy that I have described. So that's it. The only part in fact that the witness can't help with is the interview with Mr. Pasic, which I would submit would be admissible for obvious reasons, and the round-table meeting. I don't mind if the Chamber doesn't view the round-table meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber has decided that it will not at this moment seek to look at this video, which does not mean that the Chamber has decided that it would not seek further access, also in technical terms, to the video and the language spoken on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Puric, the Chamber has no further questions to you. The Prosecution had no questions for you. So where I usually say that we thank you for coming to The Hague and answering questions from Bench and parties, in this situation I have to thank you for having answered the questions of the Bench and one of the parties. Mr. Puric, it is a long way. We would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and I wish you a safe trip home again. Unfortunately you could not testify yesterday for practical reasons but we hope you'll be soon home again. And the original of your little note you will receive that through VWS, the victims and witness section, when you have left this courtroom, but we have not forgotten about it. You'll get the original back. Mr. Puric, I thank you very much for coming and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm glad that I could have made this statement because I felt it necessary to convey part of the atmosphere and also to convey our suffering and I wanted this Court to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puric, you came to answer our questions in full accordance with the truth and that's important for this Chamber. Then we will adjourn for -- we will resume at 25 minutes to 7.00. We have 25 minutes left. And then of course the Chamber will have to give a decision, if -- at least an oral decision on the second part of the motion which has been filed which was not to call a witness. We'll consider the matter. And we resume in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have only 20 minutes left for today. I take it that the next witness has become a public witness, whereas he -- we prepared his testimony, still considering the possibility of him applying for protective measures. That is a development we can't change any more. But of course the first thing we'll have to do is to give a decision on the motion that was filed only today. We considered the motion but not in full. We only considered that part of the motion where the Defence requests this Chamber not to call Mr. Djeric as a witness; whether or not the motion in relation to the evidence given by Ms. Plavsic should be granted or not is not part of our decision. The motion to the extent that it requests the Chamber and I'll then read it literally, that Mr. Branko Djeric not be called as a Chamber witness to give evidence in this trial, that motion is denied by the Chamber. The Defence might not be surprised, due to the late filing of this motion, that the reasons will be given in a written decision one of these days. But we had to -- we had to decide. Therefore, I'd like to have Mr. Djeric be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric. I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please at this moment state your full name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branko Djeric, the 20th of November, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric. Mr. Djeric, you are perhaps aware that this Tribunal has issued an indictment against you for contempt of court, and we have as well issued a warrant for your arrest which we then subsequently suspended. The reason for these contempt proceedings against you was your apparent refusal to comply with the terms of a subpoena issued to you on the 8th of June 2006. Let me first ask you are you aware of all these facts I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our registrar has copies of the subpoena, a copy of the indictment brought against you, and the arrest warrant in B/C/S. So since you say that you're not aware of it, that you now at least have copies in your own language of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I mean, you first said that an indictment was issued against me and that got me confused, you see. As for the latter part, I have to tell you that I had certain health problems that have been going on since the month of January. The problems are related to my jaw, and therefore, I have these permanent headaches. The doctors decided, since I have these implanted teeth, that a mistake must have been made at the time when the lower jaw was being worked on, and there was a mistake made. There is a discrepancy of five to six millimetres and, due to that, I do not really have a balance between my upper and lower jaw, which causes constant headaches. The pain is particularly severe around the ears and so on and so forth. So I was dealing with that all the time. And I have proof of that, you see. So that is one thing. Also, until now you communicated with me through the office of the Tribunal in Sarajevo. And then there was a certain change, I don't know why. Sometime in May, I came to the university where I work and an envelope had been left for me, a certain envelope and I asked who sent this to me said they did not know, somebody had come without any registration plates, and so on and so forth. Quite simply, I was taken aback, especially because there were provocations against me that had been going on for ten years in relation to you. I mean in relation to the Tribunal. Either by telephone or by leaving some materials for me. So you will understand that I thought that this was a provocation too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's self-evident or not is not something I think we should explore in full detail at this moment. Mr. Djeric, I just want to give you copies or at least to provide you with copies of the documents I just mentioned. The first one was an order that you should appear before this Court which you finally never got into your own hands, let me say it this way. Then the Chamber decided that it would indict and prosecute you for contempt of the Tribunal. That is, that on the 8th of June, you refused to receive a subpoena and you refused to sign a memorandum of service presented to you by an agent of Republika Srpska. At least now you've got a copy of that and on the basis of that we issued an arrest warrant and as I said before that has been suspended since then. But given that you have since decided to come to The Hague to testify in this trial of Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber has, in its discretion, decided that it is not in the interests of justice to proceed with the contempt proceedings against you. Therefore, the indictment, of which you have just received a copy, the indictment against you is hereby dismissed. At least the Chamber decides not to pursue the indictment against you any more, and as a consequence the warrant of arrest which was already suspended is hereby lifted as well. So therefore, at this moment, even though in this limited -- on these limited charges, you are no longer an accused, an accused of contempt of court before this Tribunal. And therefore, in a moment, I'll invite to you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. But before we proceed to that stage -- you've given already some of the reasons why you thought that -- why you thought that you were provoked and that you were focusing mainly on the health problems you are facing. So the Chamber -- I think it's not of major importance to further elaborate on this any more in view of the decision already taken by the Chamber. The circumstances, however, leading to your testimony in this case mean that there is no point at this stage any more to ask you in private session whether you have any reasons to apply for protective measures as a witness in the Krajisnik case. We started this whole of the procedure without making public your name and that the Chamber intended to call you as a Chamber witness, but in the contempt matter, everything became public so therefore it's no reason to ask you in private session whether you would apply for protective measures as a witness, as such, in this case. Your testimony is already a public event by now but if, in the course of your testimony, you would wish to refer to matters that might call for confidential treatment, then please let me know and we can decide such questions then on a case-by-case basis. We always have an opportunity to go into private session and to not publicly deal with certain matters. Is this all clear to you, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. I do apologise for having to use up a few minutes to thank you, because I see that you first acted as a human being and then as a lawyer. You see, nobody showed me these documents. The gentleman who came from the MUP was the person I told ultimately that I would call you. Now, was this conveyed to you? Was this conveyed to the Court? I mean, I said that I would call you as soon as I resolved my health problems. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, it might not be of great assistance to revisit the details of what happened at this moment and the Chamber has decided that it's not in the interests of justice at this moment to proceed with these contempt proceedings against you. Then this is the moment when I would like to invite you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I ask to you stand up and to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, too. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have given already your name and date of birth. That was before you made your solemn declaration. I take it that your full name and date of birth is still the same as you told us a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please state your current address and other contact details, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Pale, Pale, the street is called Ulica Srpski Ratnika, G 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: My mobile telephone number, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we should not ask you at this moment for that because people might start calling you at this moment. Perhaps at some moment, perhaps in private session and also to protect your privacy --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Please. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So perhaps if the parties or if the staff of the Chamber would need to verify these telephone numbers we will do that at a later stage but then perhaps in private session and not in public. I take it at least that the Defence would understand the reasons for that as well. Could I then ask you briefly about your educational background and may I also invite you to give concise answers? Many of the questions that will be put to you will deal with matters on which the Chamber heard already quite some evidence. Of course, the Chamber would like to hear your testimony, but sometimes there are a lot of details which are not disputed between the parties and of which the Chamber has already some knowledge. But first of all, your educational background, could you briefly state your education?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm economist by training. I have a doctorate and I'm a university professor at the school of economics. So I'm an economist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to us. Then some information about your professional become. You have -- we come later to that but on the basis of the evidence the Chamber already received we have to -- it's very likely that you'll tell us at a later stage that you were involved in politics. Could you tell us what happened before that? What was your professional background prior to entering politics or what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I started out as a young economist in a company called Energoinvest in Sarajevo. I worked there for two years. Then I became an assistant Professor at the University of Sarajevo so from then, that is to say since 1973 or rather 1974 when I became an assistant Professor to this day, I have been teaching at university. So there is a couldn't knew knit my university career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you -- whether did you enter politics for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: I was involved in politics when I was a student, for a while, as a student. And then I mean there was this void. Just before the war -- I mean, from 1974 onwards, when I came to the university and all the way up to 1991 I was not in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, how did you enter politics? I mean, what position did you then hold?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Politics. Well, I mean, I did that on behalf of the Serb political factor in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I became a member of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as minister for development, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is -- was the position you kept until the conflict broke out, is that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then once the Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you were not minister for development any more in the Bosnia-Herzegovina government, did you then enter politics in the Bosnian Serb republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As Prime Minister-designate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime round mid-March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mid-March, may I take it that it's 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, no. 1992, mid-March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. It may have been mistranslated but that is what I understood. Could you tell us where you were -- I think you already told us that later on, you went back to the university. Did you go immediately back teaching at university once you had given up your political position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: You mean in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: When I left my political position, for a while I was employed in the office of one of the Energoinvest companies in Moscow. For a while, for about four or five months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: 1993. This was 1993. And then I went back to university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not very consequent in my questions. You said that you entered politics in the Bosnian Serb republic as a designate Prime Minister in mid-March 1992. What happened -- what was your next position? Prime Minister perhaps or --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, Prime Minister-designate. That's what I mean. Prime Minister-designate and Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question would be, did you -- did you -- were you a member of any political party at that time? I'm talking about 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in activities of any political party? Even without perhaps being a member?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, I was in the League of Communists. In the League of Communists, and after that, I did not join any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djeric, I'm looking at the clock and I'm aware that you were only in this courtroom for a couple of minutes, 25 minutes until now. Nevertheless we have to stop for the day and I'd like to continue tomorrow. We would like to see you back at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom, and I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now, and the testimony still to be given in the days -- in the coming days. So you understood that instruction, I take it. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow morning, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
